pages.title: Unit 6 Rubric (teacher only)
pages.html:
Unit 6 — “Trace and Report” Rubric

Task: Trace Euclid's algorithm for a = 24, b = 9 with a full trace table; state the final output; explain each loop line in plain words; judge which error type a trace-vs-run mismatch would suggest.

Primary benchmark: SC.7.PE.3.6 (perform program tracing to predict the behavior of programs). Also evidenced: SC.7.PE.2.1 (predict outputs), SC.7.PE.1.8 (error types).

Expected trace: (24, 9) → r = 6 → (9, 6) → r = 3 → (6, 3) → r = 0 → (3, 0); the program says 3.

Criterion4 — Exemplary3 — Proficient2 — Developing1 — Beginning
Trace table (PE.3.6)Every pass present; every a/b/r value correctComplete with ≤1 arithmetic slipTable attempted; passes missing or several errorsNo usable table
Final output (PE.2.1)Correct (3), clearly statedCorrect but buriedWrong but consistent with their tableMissing/unjustified
Plain-words explanationEach loop line explained accurately in own wordsMostly accurateVague or partly wrongMissing
Error-type judgment (PE.1.8)Names a type with sound reasoning (typically logical)Names a plausible typeNames a type, weak reasoningMissing

Suggested scoring: 16 pts (4 × 4). Insincere/nonsense submissions earn no credit.

pages.title: Unit 7 Rubric (teacher only)
pages.html:
Unit 7 — Build Project Rubric (Projects 30% group)

Task: Build a Scratch program using, at least once each: a loop, a conditional, a variable the student creates and changes, an expression — plus a short deliberately non-iterative section with a one-sentence justification. Submit the project file/link and a 1–2 minute recorded walkthrough, including a one-sentence bug story.

Primary benchmark: SC.7.PE.1.6 (develop problem solutions using a block programming language — looping behavior, conditional statements, expressions, variables and functions). Also evidenced: SC.7.PE.1.11 (iterative & non-iterative structures), SC.7.PE.1.2 (iteration), SC.7.PE.1.8 (error identified in the bug story), SC.K12.CTR.1.1.

Criterion4 — Exemplary3 — Proficient2 — Developing1 — Beginning
Required elements (PE.1.6)All five present, working, and used meaningfullyAll five present and workingOne missing or non-functionalSeveral missing
Iterative + non-iterative (PE.1.11)Both present; the non-iterative choice sensibly justifiedBoth present; justification thinOne of the two missingNeither deliberate
Program qualityRuns cleanly start to finish; small and finishedRuns with minor rough edgesRuns partiallyDoes not run
Walkthrough & bug storyClear recording pointing at each element; honest bug story naming the error typeRecording covers most elements; bug story presentRecording unclear or bug story missingNo recording

Suggested scoring: 16 pts scaled to the assignment's 20 points. Ambition is welcome, but completeness beats scope. Insincere/nonsense submissions earn no credit.

pages.title: Unit 8 Rubric (teacher only)
pages.html:
Unit 8 — “Repair Report” Rubric

Task: For the three-bug program (assessment page): name each bug's type, line, and fix; name the SDLC phase whose job is catching bugs; define a class in one sentence.

Primary benchmark: SC.7.PE.1.8 (identify types of programming errors — applied in debugging). Also evidenced: SC.7.PE.4.1 (SDLC), SC.7.PE.3.4 (class concept), ELA.K12.EE.5.1.

Expected findings:

  • Line 4 — logical: total = total − s subtracts; should be +. Runs fine, answer wrong.
  • Line 5 — runtime: count was never set (0) → division by zero crashes. Fix: set count to the

number of scores (3) or guard the division.

  • Line 6 — syntax: unclosed quotation mark (and the text "aver" instead of the variable). Won't start.
  • Phase: Test (accept "testing"; maintenance also credited if reasoned as post-launch discovery).
Criterion4 — Exemplary3 — Proficient2 — Developing1 — Beginning
Bugs found & typed (PE.1.8)All three: correct type, line, and a working fixAll three found; ≤1 slip in type or fixTwo foundOne or none
FixesEach fix would truly cure the bugFixes mostly soundFixes vagueNo usable fixes
SDLC phase (PE.4.1)Test named with a reasonTest namedWrong phase, plausible reasoningMissing
Class definition (PE.3.4)One clear sentence using outline/objects/attributesAccurate definitionPartially rightMissing/wrong

Suggested scoring: 16 pts (4 × 4). Insincere/nonsense submissions earn no credit.

pages.title: Unit 9 Rubric (teacher only)
pages.html:
Unit 9 — Simulation Investigation Rubric (Projects 30% group)

Task: State a precise hypothesis; modify a simulation (the Rabbit Meadow, a PhET sim, or a Scratch simulation of the student's own) to test it fairly; record the runs; report an honest conclusion. Submitted as a short findings report + a 1–2 minute recorded walkthrough.

Primary benchmarks: SC.7.PE.3.2 (modify and create a simulation to analyze and illustrate a concept in depth) and SC.7.PE.3.3 (use modeling and simulations to test scientific hypotheses). Also evidenced: SC.7.PE.1.6 (if built in Scratch), SC.K12.CTR.6.1/7.1, MA.K12.MTR.7.1.

Criterion4 — Exemplary3 — Proficient2 — Developing1 — Beginning
Hypothesis (PE.3.3)Precise and measurable; names the parameter and the expected effectTestable, slightly looseVague claimNo real hypothesis
Fair modification (PE.3.2)One parameter (or rule) changed deliberately; the rest held; runs recorded before/afterFair test with a minor lapseMultiple things changed at onceNo controlled comparison
Data & findingsRuns recorded accurately; the comparison clearly shownRecorded with small gapsPartial dataNo usable record
Honest conclusionStates supported/refuted exactly, notes the model's limits (what it leaves out)Correct verdictVerdict unclear or overstatedConclusion contradicts the data

Suggested scoring: 16 pts scaled to the assignment's 20 points. A refuted hypothesis honestly reported scores as well as a supported one. Insincere/nonsense submissions earn no credit.

pages.title: Unit 10 Rubric (teacher only)

Unit 10 — Capstone Portfolio Rubric (Projects 30% group · final entry)

Task: A published digital portfolio (welcome page + 4–6 artifacts from across the year, each with an introduction naming the skill it shows and one lesson learned; tools and sources credited), plus a 2–4 minute recorded presentation and the final written reflection (good/true/beautiful + the virtue it demanded).

assignments.title: Lesson 1 Discussion — Can Machines Think?
assignments.html:
This is an online discussion. Read the assigned opening of Turing's "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" (1950) and one objection of your choice — the "Lady Lovelace" objection connects directly to Unit 5.

Where to find the reading: open the Unit 6 Reading — “Turing: Can Machines Think?” page in this module. It links the free full text and tells you exactly which parts to read (the opening on the imitation game, plus one objection from the section “Contrary Views on the Main Question”). Direct link to the reading: archive.org — Computing Machinery and Intelligence ↗ (free, no account).

Post to the discussion board, then reply to a classmate:

  1. In your own words, why did Turing replace "Can machines think?" with the imitation game?
  2. State the objection you read, and Turing's reply to it — then say whether you find his reply convincing, with a reason.
  3. Reply thoughtfully to at least one classmate — especially one who chose a different objection.

You may type, upload, or record your response.

Graded on: an accurate account of the game; a fair summary of one objection and reply; your own reasoned judgment; a courteous, substantive reply to a peer.

assignments.title: Lesson 2 Activity — Trace It Yourself
assignments.html:
You watched the trace stepper run Euclid's algorithm. Now trace it yourself.

Submit (text, file, or media):

  1. Trace Euclid's algorithm for a = 36, b = 10. Write the full trace table — one row per pass, with the values of a, b, and r — and state what the program says.
  2. Trace it again for a pair of numbers you choose.
  3. In one sentence: what tells you the loop is about to stop?

Graded on: complete, correct trace tables; correct final outputs; the stop condition identified.

assignments.title: Lesson 3 Activity — Sections in Your Own Words
assignments.html:
You matched the password randomizer's sections to their purposes. Now write it out properly — the way a programmer documents unfamiliar code.

Submit (text, file, or media):

  1. For each of the four sections of the password program, write 1–2 sentences in your own words predicting what that section will do when the program runs.
  2. Predict the program's behavior for input length = 3: how many characters, and does the warning appear?
  3. Suppose Section 3's loop said repeat length − 1 times by mistake. Predict what would change — and name the error type.

Graded on: accurate own-words predictions per section; correct behavior predictions; the off-by-one identified as a logical error.

assignments.title: Lesson 4 Activity — Three Kinds of Wrong
assignments.html:
You classified errors as syntax, logical, or runtime.

Submit (text, file, or media):

  1. Define the three error types in your own words — one sentence each — including when each shows itself (won't start / won't finish / finishes wrong).
  2. Invent one example of each type (a line of code, or a plain description of what goes wrong).
  3. Which type is hardest to find, and what skill from this unit finds it?

Graded on: accurate definitions; three sensible, correctly-typed examples; the logical-error + tracing connection.

assignments.title: Unit 6 Build — The Trace Wall (Arthur VR)
assignments.html:
Build a small "trace wall" — a program and its trace, laid out in space. You create it yourself — nothing to "join." Plan on about 20–30 minutes.

Build it in Arthur (VR):

  1. Create your own space in Arthur.
  2. Post a tiny program (3–4 lines — Euclid for small numbers, or a short loop from Unit 5) on one panel.
  3. Next to it, build its trace table as a row of notes: one note per pass, showing each variable's value.
  4. Add one "wanted poster" note for an error type of your choice — its name, how it shows itself, and a one-line example.
  5. Record a 1–2 minute walkthrough reading your trace aloud, pass by pass, ending with what the program says.

No headset? Do the no-VR version (same credit): one slide or short doc with the program, its trace table, and the error-type "wanted poster."

Submit: your recording (link/upload) or your slide/doc. You may type, upload, or record media.

Graded on: a correct trace of your program; the final output stated; an accurate error-type poster; a clear walkthrough in your own words. Keep it simple and neat.

assignments.title: Lesson 1 Discussion — Patterns You Have Seen
assignments.html:
This is an online discussion about the patterns around you.

Post to the discussion board, then reply to a classmate:

  1. Describe one repeating pattern you have met — in nature, music, art, sports, or daily life.
  2. State its rule the way we stated Fibonacci's ("each new number is the sum of the two before"): what is the repeated step?
  3. Could a loop build your pattern? Say what the loop body would do.
  4. Reply thoughtfully to at least one classmate — try continuing their pattern by its rule.

You may type, upload, or record your response.

Graded on: a real pattern with a precisely stated rule; a sensible loop connection; a courteous, substantive reply.

assignments.title: Lesson 2 Activity — Loops With a Purpose
assignments.html:
You assembled a loop and studied its behavior.

Submit (text, file, or media):

  1. Write (pseudocode or block-style) a loop that says every item of a list you invent — at least four items.
  2. For your loop, answer the two loop questions: what step repeats? and what makes it stop?
  3. Write one loop that would run forever — and one sentence on why, naming the error type.

Graded on: a working for-each loop; both loop questions answered; the infinite loop correctly explained as a logical error.

assignments.title: Lesson 3 Activity — Fibonacci, Both Ways
assignments.html:
You watched the sequence built two ways. Now create both structures yourself.

Submit (text, file, or media):

  1. Non-iterative: write out the steps (no loop) that produce the first 7 Fibonacci numbers, one line per new term.
  2. Iterative: write a loop version (pseudocode or block-style) that produces the same 7 numbers.
  3. Count the lines in each. Which version would you trust for 50 terms, and why — in two sentences?

Graded on: both structures correct and clearly distinct; accurate terms (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13); a sound comparison.

assignments.title: Lesson 4 Activity — Five Powers in Scratch
assignments.html:
Open Scratch (press Create — no sign-in needed) and explore the five powers.

Submit (text, file, or media — screenshots welcome):

  1. Build a tiny script that uses a loop, a variable, and a conditional together (the Lesson 4 example script is a fine starting point).
  2. Screenshot or describe your script, and state what it does when it runs.
  3. Find one expression block (Operators) and one My Block (function). Name each and say, in one sentence, what job it does.

Graded on: a working three-power script; an accurate account of its behavior; correct identification of an expression and a function.

assignments.title: Unit 7 Project — Build With the Five Powers
assignments.html:
Your first major project: build a program of your own in Scratch. What it is — a pattern-drawer, a quiz game, a Fibonacci machine, a story with choices — is your call. Small and finished beats big and broken.

Your program must use, at least once each:

  1. a loop (iterative structure),
  2. a conditional (if… then),
  3. a variable you create and change,
  4. an expression that computes something,
  5. a short non-iterative section — steps deliberately written out — with a one-sentence note on why you chose not to loop there.

Submit:

  • Your project — a shared link, or the file from File → Save to your computer;
  • a 1–2 minute recorded walkthrough: show it running and point at each required element;
  • your bug story — one sentence about something that went wrong while building, naming the error type (syntax, logical, or runtime) and how you fixed it.

Graded with the Unit 7 project rubric: all five elements present and working · iterative + non-iterative both deliberate · runs cleanly · clear walkthrough and honest bug story. This project counts in the Projects portion of your grade.

assignments.title: Unit 7 Build — Fibonacci Garden (Arthur VR)
assignments.html:
Build a small "Fibonacci garden" — the sequence growing through space. You create it yourself — nothing to "join." Plan on about 20–30 minutes.

Build it in Arthur (VR):

  1. Create your own space in Arthur.
  2. Place labeled markers for the first 8 Fibonacci numbers (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21) in a row or spiral — let the spacing or size grow with the numbers if you like.
  3. Add one note stating the rule ("each number is the sum of the two before").
  4. Add one note contrasting the two ways to build it: iterative — one repeated step vs. non-iterative — every step written out.
  5. Record a 1–2 minute walkthrough reading the sequence aloud and explaining, at one marker, how it was made from the two before.

No headset? Do the no-VR version (same credit): one slide or short doc with the 8 labeled numbers (a drawn spiral is welcome), the rule, and the iterative-vs-non-iterative note.

Submit: your recording (link/upload) or your slide/doc. You may type, upload, or record media.

Graded on: correct sequence and rule; an accurate iterative-vs-non-iterative note; a clear walkthrough in your own words. Keep it simple and neat.

assignments.title: Lesson 1 Discussion — The Moth in the Log
assignments.html:
This is an online discussion. Look closely at the 1947 logbook page — the moth is still taped to it.

Where to find it: open the Unit 8 Primary Source — “The First Computer Bug” page in this module. Direct link to the artifact: Smithsonian — Log Book With Computer Bug ↗.

Post to the discussion board, then reply to a classmate:

  1. Why do you think the engineers kept the moth and wrote the note, instead of just fixing the machine and moving on? What does an honest record do for the next person?
  2. Tell a short "bug story" of your own — a time something you made (code, a recipe, a build, a routine) went wrong. Name which error type it most resembles: wouldn't start, wouldn't finish, or finished wrong.
  3. Reply thoughtfully to at least one classmate — suggest how you would have hunted their bug.

You may type, upload, or record your response.

Graded on: a thoughtful reading of the artifact; a bug story with a correct error-type match; a courteous, substantive reply.

assignments.title: Lesson 2 Activity — One Turn of the Wheel
assignments.html:
You ordered the six phases and matched activities to them.

Submit (text, file, or media):

  1. List the six phases of the software development life cycle, in order, with one sentence defining each.
  2. Take a project you have actually made — your Unit 7 Scratch build is perfect — and describe one thing you did in each phase (even informally). If you skipped a phase, say so honestly and note what skipping it cost you.
  3. In one sentence: why is it a cycle and not a straight line?

Graded on: all six phases correctly defined and ordered; an honest mapping of your own project onto the cycle; the cycle explained.

assignments.title: Lesson 3 Activity — Design a Class
assignments.html:
You sorted blueprints from the things built from them. Now design one.

Submit (text, file, or media):

  1. Define a class in one sentence of your own, using the words outline, objects, and attributes.
  2. Choose a kind of thing a program might track (a player, a plant, a song, a pet…). Write its class: the class name and three sensible attributes.
  3. Create two objects from your class — same attributes, each with its own values.
  4. In one sentence: what stays the same between your two objects, and what differs?

Graded on: an accurate definition; a well-chosen class with sensible attributes; two correct objects; the same/different insight.

assignments.title: Unit 8 Build — The Software Workshop (Arthur VR)
assignments.html:
Build a small "software workshop" — the life cycle laid out as stations. You create it yourself — nothing to "join." Plan on about 20–30 minutes.

Build it in Arthur (VR):

  1. Create your own space in Arthur.
  2. Place six labeled stations in order — Plan, Design, Build, Test, Launch, Maintain — each with one note saying what happens there.
  3. At the Test station, add a small "bug board": the three error types with your one-line memory aid for each (won't start / won't finish / finishes wrong).
  4. Optional flourish: a "moth in the log" tribute note at Test — the 1947 story in one sentence.
  5. Record a 1–2 minute walkthrough touring the six stations in order.

No headset? Do the no-VR version (same credit): one slide or short doc with the six phases in order (one line each) and the three-error bug board.

Submit: your recording (link/upload) or your slide/doc. You may type, upload, or record media.

Graded on: six phases correct and in order with accurate one-liners; a correct bug board; a clear walkthrough in your own words. Keep it simple and neat.

assignments.title: Lesson 1 Discussion — Models Around You
assignments.html:
This is an online discussion about the models and simulations already in your life.

Post to the discussion board, then reply to a classmate:

  1. Name one model or simulation you have actually used — a weather forecast, a flight or driving simulator, a sports video game, a map, a science sim.
  2. What does it keep from the real world, and what does it leave out?
  3. Does the omission matter for how people use it? Give one case where trusting the model too far could mislead someone.
  4. Reply thoughtfully to at least one classmate — suggest one more thing their model omits.

You may type, upload, or record your response.

Graded on: a real model correctly described; a thoughtful keep/omit analysis; a courteous, substantive reply.

assignments.title: Lesson 2 Activity — Three Fates of the Meadow
assignments.html:
You turned the meadow's dials. Now document what you found.

Submit (text, file, or media — screenshots of your runs welcome):

  1. Find and record parameter settings (starting rabbits + food) that make the herd (a) grow, (b) shrink, and (c) hold steady from the very first round. List all three settings with the first three rounds of each run.
  2. In 2–3 sentences: what concept does this simulation illustrate about populations and resources? (Hint: what happens to every growing herd eventually?)
  3. Propose one rule change (not a dial — a change to the model's rules) and predict how it would alter the meadow's behavior.

Graded on: three correct settings with accurate runs; the carrying-capacity insight in your own words; a sensible rule-change proposal with a prediction.

assignments.title: Unit 9 Project — The Simulation Investigation
assignments.html:
Your major project this unit: a real investigation. You will use a simulation the way a scientist does — hypothesis first, honest report last.

Choose your laboratory (any one):

  • the Rabbit Meadow from Lessons 2–3;
  • a free PhET simulation (phet.colorado.edu — no account needed; ask your teacher if unsure which);
  • or — for an extra challenge — a small simulation you build yourself in Scratch (a loop turning rounds, variables for the state, a rule or two).

The investigation (four steps):

  1. State a hypothesis — precise and testable: name the parameter you will change and the effect you expect, with numbers where you can.
  2. Predict the outcome before running.
  3. Run a fair test — change only that one parameter; record the runs (screenshots or a table).
  4. Conclude honestly — supported or refuted? Note one thing your model leaves out that could matter in the real world.

Submit: your findings report (the four steps, written out) plus a 1–2 minute recorded walkthrough showing a run and stating your conclusion. You may type, upload files, or record media.

Graded with the Unit 9 project rubric: precise hypothesis · fair modification · accurate record · honest conclusion. A refuted hypothesis honestly reported scores just as well as a supported one. This project counts in the Projects portion of your grade.

assignments.title: Unit 9 Build — The Model Museum (Arthur VR)
assignments.html:
Build a small "model museum" — one exhibit about a model and what it teaches. You create it yourself — nothing to "join." Plan on about 20–30 minutes.

Build it in Arthur (VR):

  1. Create your own space in Arthur.
  2. Make an exhibit for one model or simulation (the Rabbit Meadow, a PhET sim, a weather forecast, a flight simulator…). Include three labeled panels: what it models, what it keeps, and what it leaves out.
  3. Add a fourth panel with the four-step investigation: state → predict → run fairly → conclude honestly.
  4. Record a 1–2 minute walkthrough touring your exhibit in your own words.

No headset? Do the no-VR version (same credit): one slide or short doc with the same four panels.

Submit: your recording (link/upload) or your slide/doc. You may type, upload, or record media.

Graded on: an accurate keeps/omits analysis; the four investigation steps correct and in order; a clear walkthrough in your own words. Keep it simple and neat.

assignments.title: Lesson 1 Discussion — Vague, but Exciting
assignments.html:
This is an online discussion. Read the opening sections of Tim Berners-Lee's 1989 proposal (w3.org/History/1989/proposal.html) — the memo his boss marked "Vague, but exciting."

Post to the discussion board, then reply to a classmate:

  1. In your own words: what problem at CERN was the proposal trying to solve?
  2. Why do you think his boss called it both vague AND exciting? Was the boss right on both counts?
  3. Berners-Lee gave the Web away instead of patenting it. Name one way your life this year used that gift — and whether you think his choice was the right one.
  4. Reply thoughtfully to at least one classmate.

You may type, upload, or record your response.

Graded on: an accurate account of the problem; a reasoned reading of "vague, but exciting"; a thoughtful judgment on the giving-away; a courteous, substantive reply.

assignments.title: Lesson 2 Activity — Build a Practice Page
assignments.html:
Time to create real online content — one page, built with care. It will become a draft section of your capstone portfolio.

Build one page in a school-approved design tool (your teacher will name it — e.g., Google Sites) or in plain HTML if you prefer, introducing one project from your year (your Scratch build and your simulation investigation are strong choices).

Your page must have:

  1. a clear title heading and at least one section heading;
  2. a short paragraph saying what the project is and what skill it shows;
  3. at least one image (screenshot) with alt text;
  4. at least one link (to the project itself, or a related page);
  5. readable contrast and restrained design — the four rules from the lesson.

Submit: the page link, or screenshots plus your file. You may also record a short walkthrough.

Graded on: all five required elements present; design that follows the four rules; writing in your own voice.

assignments.title: Lesson 4 Discussion — Warm & Cool Feedback
assignments.html:
This is an online discussion — the peer-feedback round for draft portfolios.

Post and reply on the discussion board:

  1. Post your draft portfolio link (or screenshots of your pages so far) with one sentence on what you would like feedback about.
  2. Visit two classmates' drafts. For each, leave one warm comment (specific: name what works and why) and one cool comment (a courteous, specific question or suggestion).
  3. Close your own post with a career note: after this year, which technology career path interests you most, and which portfolio artifact points toward it?

You may type, upload, or record your comments.

Graded on: a shared draft; two rounds of specific warm + cool feedback about the work (never the person); a reasoned career note.

assignments.title: Capstone Portfolio — Digital Discoveries
assignments.html:
The Capstone Portfolio — the year's largest single grade, and its proudest. Everything you have practiced comes together here: design, honesty, voice, and a year of real work.

Part 1 — the published portfolio (built in your school-approved design tool):

  1. a welcome page — who you are as a maker, in a few honest sentences;
  2. 4–6 artifacts from across the year, each showing a different skill (your Lesson 3 labels will guide you);
  3. an introduction for each artifact: what it is, the skill it shows, and one thing you learned making it;
  4. clean, accessible design throughout — headings, contrast, alt text on every image, restraint;
  5. credit for the tools you used and anything you built upon.

Part 2 — the recorded presentation (2–4 minutes, media recording or upload): welcome → two artifacts examined closely → your year in one thought. Your own voice, unhurried.

Part 3 — the final reflection (a short paragraph, typed or recorded): Was the work of your year good, true, and beautiful — and which virtue did it demand most of you?

Submit: the portfolio link (or files), your recording, and your reflection. You may type, upload files, or record media.

Graded with the Capstone rubric: curation · craft & accessibility · the recorded presentation · honesty and credit. This assignment counts in the Projects portion of your grade. Small, finished, and honest — as always.

assignments.title: Unit 10 Build — Portfolio Gallery (Arthur VR)
assignments.html:
Your final build: a small gallery of your own year. You create it yourself — nothing to "join." Plan on about 20–30 minutes.

Build it in Arthur (VR):

  1. Create your own space in Arthur — your personal gallery.
  2. Hang three exhibits: your three favorite artifacts from the year (screenshots or notes), each with a museum label — its name, its unit, and the skill it shows.
  3. Add one "about the maker" panel: your name and one sentence on how you have changed as a maker since August.
  4. Record a 1–2 minute walkthrough touring your gallery — your last recording of the year. Make it a proud one.

No headset? Do the no-VR version (same credit): one slide or short doc with the three labeled exhibits and the about-the-maker panel.

Submit: your recording (link/upload) or your slide/doc. You may type, upload, or record media.

Graded on: three well-labeled exhibits from different units; an honest about-the-maker panel; a clear walkthrough in your own words. Keep it simple, neat — and yours.

questions.text: What does it mean to trace a program?

answers.text: Run it as fast as possible
Delete the lines you don't understand
Follow it by hand, line by line, recording each variable's value as it changes
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — tracing is being the computer, one line at a time, with a trace table.

answers.text: Guess the output from the program's name

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Tracing means following the code by hand and recording every variable change.

questions.text: Trace this program: x = 3, then x = x × 2, then x = x + 1. What is x at the end?

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — 3 → 6 → 7.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Trace it: x = 3; ×2 makes 6; +1 makes 7.

questions.text: Euclid's algorithm: while b is not 0 → r = remainder of a ÷ b; a = b; b = r; then say a. Trace it for a = 20, b = 8. What does it say?
questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Trace: 20÷8 leaves 4 → (8,4); 8÷4 leaves 0 → (4,0). It says 4.

questions.text: A password program repeats length times, adding one random character each pass. Input: length = 4. What can you predict about the output?

answers.text: The exact password it will print
It will have exactly 4 characters — though which characters is random
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — understanding the input lets you predict the shape of the output.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ The loop runs length times — so 4 characters, even though each one is random.

questions.text: The program warns when length < 8. For which input does the warning appear?

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — 5 < 8 is true, so the warning is said.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Only inputs below 8 trigger the warning: 5 < 8 is true; 8 and 12 are not below 8.

questions.text: Why do programmers predict a program's outputs before running it?

answers.text: It proves they truly understand what the inputs do — and catches wrong thinking early
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — comparing prediction to reality is how understanding is tested.

answers.text: Predictions replace the need to ever run the program

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Predicting outputs shows understanding of inputs — and reveals mistakes in thinking.

questions.text: say "Hello — the closing quotation mark is missing, and the program refuses to start. Which error type is this?

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — broken grammar the computer rejects before running is a syntax error.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ "Won't start" = syntax: the code breaks the language's grammar.

questions.text: A grade calculator runs from start to finish with no complaints — but gives every student 10 points too many. Which error type is this?

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — "finishes wrong" is a logical error; only a trace or test reveals it.

answers.text: No error — the students earned it

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ It runs fine but the answer is wrong — a logical error.

questions.text: A program starts fine, then crashes halfway through when it divides by zero. Which error type is this?

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — it began running and hit something impossible: runtime.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ "Won't finish" = runtime: a legal program that hits an impossible operation mid-run.

questions.text: Trace Euclid's algorithm by hand for a = 24, b = 9: write the full trace table (every pass: a, b, r), state what the program says, and explain each loop line in your own words. Finish with one sentence: if your trace disagreed with the real run, which error type would you suspect first, and why? (Graded with the Unit 6 rubric.)
In the Fibonacci sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, … each new number is made by…

answers.text: adding the two numbers before it
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — each term is the sum of the previous two.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ The Fibonacci rule: add the two numbers before. 5 + 8 = 13.

questions.text: A code segment is iterative when it…

answers.text: writes every step out one after another
uses a loop to repeat a step
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — iterative means a loop repeats the step.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Iterative = uses a loop; non-iterative = steps written out with no repetition structure.

questions.text: You need the first 100 Fibonacci numbers. Compared with writing each step out, an iterative version…

answers.text: needs the same few lines no matter how many terms you want
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — the loop's few lines serve any length; only the count changes.

answers.text: needs one new line for every extra term

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Both versions give the same numbers — but the loop stays a few lines at any length.

questions.text: for each animal of [cat, dog, owl]: say animal — what happens?

answers.text: It says cat, then dog, then owl
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — the loop visits each element in order, and the variable takes each value.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ For-each visits every element in order: cat, dog, owl.

questions.text: Every loop must answer two questions. Which pair is it?

answers.text: What step repeats? What makes it stop?
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — the repeated step and the stopping condition define every loop.

answers.text: Who wrote it? When was it written?

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ A loop is defined by what repeats and what stops it — forget the second and you loop forever.

questions.text: True or False: A loop whose stopping condition can never become true is an infinite loop — a logical error.

answers.feedback: ✅ True — the program runs, but never toward its goal: a logical error.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ It’s true — if nothing moves the condition toward true, the loop never ends.

questions.text: In a block language like Scratch, if (score > 10) then say "You win!" is a…

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — if-then acts only when its condition is true: a conditional.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ An if-then block is a conditional statement.

questions.text: In Scratch, a “My Block” — a stack of blocks you name once and reuse by name — is the block language’s version of a…

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — named, reusable steps are a function.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Naming a stack of blocks to reuse anywhere is a function (“My Blocks”).

questions.text: Trace this block script: set score to 0; repeat 5 times: change score by 2; say score. What is said?

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — five passes × change by 2 = 10.

questions.text: The word debugging traces back to 1947, when engineers on Grace Hopper's Mark II team…

answers.text: found an actual moth in a relay and taped it into the logbook
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — "First actual case of bug being found," moth included.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ The 1947 logbook holds a real moth — the famous "first actual case of bug being found."

questions.text: A savings app runs perfectly but shows a total that is always a little too high. As a systematic debugger, you suspect a…

answers.text: syntax error — check for missing quotes
runtime error — it must be crashing
logical error — trace the math to find where it disobeys the intent
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — runs but finishes wrong = logical; tracing finds it.

answers.text: hardware error — buy a new computer

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ It runs to the end with a wrong answer — the signature of a logical error.

questions.text: Which is the systematic way to debug?

answers.text: Observe what goes wrong → locate it (trace) → name the error type → fix one thing and re-test
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — observe, locate, name, fix-and-retest.

answers.text: Change many lines at once and hope
Delete the program and start over every time

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Systematic debugging: observe → locate → name the type → fix ONE thing and re-test.

questions.text: Which lists the phases of the software development life cycle in order?

answers.text: Build → Plan → Launch → Design → Test → Maintain
Test → Build → Design → Plan → Maintain → Launch
Launch → Maintain → Plan → Design → Build → Test
Plan → Design → Build → Test → Launch → Maintain
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — plan, design, build, test, launch, maintain.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ The cycle runs: Plan → Design → Build → Test → Launch → Maintain.

questions.text: Sketching every screen of an app on paper before writing any code belongs to which phase?

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — deciding HOW before building is design.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Sketching how it will work, before code, is the design phase.

questions.text: True or False: The life cycle is called a cycle because the maintain phase often feeds new plans — the wheel turns again.

answers.feedback: ✅ True — maintenance discoveries become the next plan.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ It’s true — that loop from maintain back to plan is why it is a cycle, not a line.

questions.text: In object-oriented programming, a class is best described as…

answers.text: the outline — the blueprint — from which objects are made
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — a class is the outline for objects and their attributes.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ A class is the blueprint/outline from which objects are made.

questions.text: A Dog class lists name, age, and breed. The dog rex — "Rex", 3, beagle is…

answers.text: an object made from the class, with its own attribute values
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — one thing built from the outline, values filled in.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ rex is an object: made from the Dog class, with his own values.

questions.text: In the Dog class, name, age, and breed are called its…

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — the class outlines its objects' attributes.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ The properties a class lists for its objects are attributes.

questions.text: Write the repair report for the three-bug program on the Unit 8 Assessment page: for each bug give its type, its line, and the fix. Then name the SDLC phase whose job is catching bugs, and define a class in one sentence of your own. (Graded with the Unit 8 rubric.)
A simulation is best described as…

answers.text: a photograph of the real world
a model set in motion by a program, step by step
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — rules, variables, and a loop, run step by step.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ A simulation is a model run by a program, step by step.

questions.text: In the Rabbit Meadow, changing food per round from 20 to 40 is an example of…

answers.text: modifying a parameter of the simulation
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — parameters are the model's dials; turning one modifies the simulation.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Values set before a run are parameters — changing one modifies the simulation.

questions.text: Every model leaves things out (the meadow has no foxes or winters). This is…

answers.text: deliberate focus — keep what matters for the question, and know the limits
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — simplification is the strength, and the caution.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Good models simplify on purpose — and honest users remember what was left out.

questions.text: Which is a testable hypothesis for the meadow?

answers.text: "If food doubles from 20 to 40, the settled herd will double."
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — specific and measurable, so a run can support or refute it.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ A hypothesis must be specific and testable — like the doubling claim.

questions.text: To fairly test whether food changes the herd's fate, you should…

answers.text: change only the food parameter, keeping everything else the same
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — one change per test, or you cannot name the cause.

answers.text: change food AND starting rabbits at once
edit the rules and the dials together

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ A fair test changes ONE parameter and holds the rest steady.

questions.text: True or False: If a simulation refutes your hypothesis, the honest step is to report the refutation exactly — not to adjust the numbers until they agree.

answers.feedback: ✅ True — the model shows what it shows; report it.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ It’s true — honesty about refutations is the discipline of science.

questions.text: The meadow's rule — if food ≥ needed + 4: rabbits = rabbits + 2 — is built from which block-language powers?

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — if-then (conditional), ≥ and + (expressions), rabbits/food/needed (variables).

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ The rule is a conditional using expressions and variables — a simulation IS a program.

questions.text: Which block-language structure turns the meadow's world one round at a time?

answers.text: a loop — each pass is one round
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — the loop advances the simulation round by round.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ The loop — each pass of its body is one round of the simulated world.

questions.text: Trace the meadow: 10 rabbits, food 16. After round 1, then round 2, the herd is… (needed = rabbits × 2; shortage → −2; just enough → steady)

answers.text: 8, then 8 — it shrinks once, then holds
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — needed 20 > 16 → 8; then needed 16 = food → steady at 8.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Trace it: needed 20 > 16 → down to 8; then needed 16 = 16 → steady. 8, then 8.

questions.text: Tim Berners-Lee's 1989 proposal — the one his boss called "vague, but exciting" — became…

answers.text: the World Wide Web — pages joined by hyperlinks
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — and he gave it away for everyone to build on.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ The 1989 CERN proposal became the World Wide Web.

questions.text: Which are examples of online content you can create with design tools?

answers.text: Webpages, digital portfolios, and multimedia artifacts
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — webpages, portfolios, and multimedia artifacts.

answers.text: Nothing without writing raw HTML by hand

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Online content includes webpages, digital portfolios and multimedia artifacts — and design tools handle the HTML for you.

questions.text: In HTML, the tag <a href="project.html">See more</a> creates…

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — the hyperlink, Berners-Lee's whole idea.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ The <a href> tag is the hyperlink — pages joined to pages.

questions.text: A well-designed portfolio page has…

answers.text: seven fonts and a blinking border
pale yellow text on white, for softness
images without alt text, to save time
clear headings, readable contrast, alt text on images, and restraint
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — design that serves every reader.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Headings in order, readable contrast, alt text, and less-but-better.

questions.text: Your team is building one shared multimedia page. The collaborative way is…

answers.text: emailing copies back and forth and merging by hand
using the tool's sharing — one page, everyone editing with their own role
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — one shared artifact, edited together (Unit 2's lesson, applied).

answers.text: printing it and gluing pieces together

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Multimedia tools are built for collaboration: one shared page, everyone contributing.

questions.text: True or False: Specific warm feedback ("your hypothesis is stated so clearly I could predict the chart") helps a maker more than "I like it."

answers.feedback: ✅ True — specific feedback names what works, so the maker can keep doing it.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ It's true — specificity is what makes feedback usable.

questions.text: A person who builds and maintains webpages — sweating headings, contrast, and alt text — works as a…

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — the craft you practiced building your portfolio.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Building and maintaining online content is the web developer's daily work.

questions.text: To analyze a technology career path well, you examine…

answers.text: what the job does day to day, the preparation it needs, and its outlook — from a reliable source
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — duties, preparation, outlook, from a source like the BLS Handbook.

answers.text: nothing — you pick one at random

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Analysis looks at the work itself, the preparation, and the outlook — from reliable sources.

questions.text: A classmate loved the Unit 9 investigation — forming hypotheses and testing them against models. Which career path fits that love best?

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct — hypotheses, models, and honest findings are that path's daily bread.

questions.feedback_incorrect: ❌ Testing hypotheses against models is the heart of data and simulation science.
